title: Jeremiah 15:1–9
context: The LORD tells Jeremiah that even Moses and Samuel could not turn him toward this people now, and announces sword, famine, captivity, and four kinds of destroyers. He links the judgment to Manasseh’s sins, as 2 Kings 21:10–16, 23:26–27, and 24:3–4 also do, while stressing the people’s own refusal to return. These hard words concern Judah’s judgment in that hour, not individual salvation, and both traditions read them that way. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about judgment after long patience.

verses.text: Then the LORD said to me, “Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, yet my mind would not turn toward this people. Cast them out of my sight, and let them go out!
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD tells Jeremiah that even if Moses and Samuel stood before him, his mind would not turn toward this people: cast them out. The word is severe.

Arminian readers see judgment that intercession can no longer avert (compare the boxes at Joshua 10:14 and Exodus 32:14).
verses.reformedNotes:
Moses and Samuel were remembered as great intercessors (compare Exodus 32:11–14; 1 Samuel 12:23).

Reformed readers see God’s settled decree. Both traditions read it as a word about Judah’s judgment in that hour, not about individual salvation.

verses.text: It will happen when they ask you, ‘Where shall we go out?’ then you shall tell them, ‘The LORD says: “Such as are for death, to death; such as are for the sword, to the sword; such as are for the famine, to the famine; and such as are for captivity, to captivity.” ’
verses.arminianNotes:
When the people ask where they should go, Jeremiah is to tell them: some to death, some to the sword, some to famine, some to captivity. Each faces judgment.

Arminian readers see the stark consequences of persistent rebellion.
verses.reformedNotes:
The fourfold pattern is grim, and the text states it plainly.

Reformed readers see the certainty of God’s judgment once pronounced. Both traditions read this soberly as shared ground and hear in it the seriousness of the coming disaster.

verses.text: “I will appoint over them four kinds,” says the LORD: “the sword to kill, the dogs to tear, the birds of the sky, and the animals of the earth, to devour and to destroy.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD appoints four kinds of destroyers over them: the sword to kill, dogs to tear, birds and animals to devour. Judgment is complete.

Arminian readers see covenant curses coming upon a people who refused to return.
verses.reformedNotes:
The imagery resembles covenant curse language found elsewhere in Scripture, and its severity is meant to be felt.

Reformed readers see God’s justice against persistent sin. Both traditions read this soberly as shared ground about the seriousness of judgment.

verses.text: I will cause them to be tossed back and forth among all the kingdoms of the earth, because of Manasseh, the son of Hezekiah, king of Judah, for that which he did in Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will make them a horror among the kingdoms because of what Manasseh son of Hezekiah did in Jerusalem. The judgment has a history.

Arminian readers see accumulated sin bearing consequences across generations.
verses.reformedNotes:
2 Kings 21:10–16, 23:26–27, and 24:3–4 likewise trace Judah’s fall to Manasseh’s sins; Jeremiah also stresses the people’s own refusal to return (15:7).

Reformed readers see God’s long patience ending. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: For who will have pity on you, Jerusalem? Who will mourn you? Who will come to ask of your welfare?
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD asks who will pity Jerusalem, mourn for her, or ask about her welfare. The city is left alone.

Arminian readers see the loneliness that follows rejecting God, who had been Jerusalem’s true protector and friend.
verses.reformedNotes:
The questions express the depth of Jerusalem’s isolation.

Reformed readers see the consequences of forsaking the LORD. Both traditions read this as shared ground and hear in the questions a note of sorrow even within the announcement of judgment.

verses.text: You have rejected me,” says the LORD. “You have gone backward. Therefore I have stretched out my hand against you and destroyed you. I am weary of showing compassion.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “You have rejected me,” and “You have gone backward,” so he has stretched out his hand against them; he is weary of showing compassion. The rejection is mutual.

Arminian readers see judgment answering Judah’s own rejection.
verses.reformedNotes:
God’s weariness of compassion follows long patience; how God’s compassion relates to judgment is treated at the Judges 10:16 box.

Reformed readers see patience exhausted. Both traditions read it as a word about Judah’s judgment, not about individual salvation.

verses.text: I have winnowed them with a fan in the gates of the land. I have bereaved them of children. I have destroyed my people. They didn’t return from their ways.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD has winnowed them in the gates of the land, bereaved them, and destroyed his people, for they did not return from their ways. Judgment follows refusal.

Arminian readers see the stated cause: they did not return.
verses.reformedNotes:
Winnowing separates grain from chaff, an image of sifting judgment.

Reformed readers see God’s discipline of his people. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the consequences of refusing to repent, which the verse names directly as the reason for judgment.

verses.text: Their widows are increased more than the sand of the seas. I have brought on them against the mother of the young men a destroyer at noonday. I have caused anguish and terrors to fall on her suddenly.
verses.arminianNotes:
Widows are more numerous than the sand of the seas, and a destroyer comes at noon against the mother of young men, with sudden anguish and terror. The grief is vast.

Arminian readers see the human cost of war.
verses.reformedNotes:
The image of widows beyond counting reverses the promise of descendants like the sand (compare Genesis 22:17), as some readers suggest.

Reformed readers see judgment’s sorrow. Both traditions read this soberly as shared ground.

verses.text: She who has borne seven languishes. She has given up the spirit. Her sun has gone down while it was yet day. She has been disappointed and confounded. I will deliver their residue to the sword before their enemies,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
She who bore seven languishes and breathes her last; her sun sets while it is still day, and the remnant will fall by the sword. Hope seems extinguished.

Arminian readers see grief expressed through the image of a bereaved mother.
verses.reformedNotes:
A mother of seven, a picture of blessing, now faces loss. The image is poignant and sorrowful.

Reformed readers see the depth of judgment’s sorrow. Both traditions read this soberly and pastorally as shared ground.
